extracted.intended_audience: general Wikipedia readers, fans of the show, and readers interested in TV panel show formats
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the format, rounds, scoring and production constraints of the British comedy panel show Would I Lie to You?, including rules for each round and how episodes are recorded and edited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show format: teams and premise
rubrics_metrics.description: For each show, two celebrity guests join each of the team captains. The teams compete as each player reveals unusual facts and embarrassing personal tales for the evaluation of the opposing team. Some of these are true, some are not, and it is the panellists' task to decide which is which.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic format allows each team member to question and joke with the opposing team; improvisation and humorous questioning are central to the show's entertainment value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring system
rubrics_metrics.description: In all rounds, the scoring system is the same: teams gain a point for correctly guessing whether a statement is true or not, but if they guess incorrectly the opposing team gets a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each episode running time is 30 minutes, so some questions are edited out prior to airing. Hence, episodes have differing total scoring points reflecting the varying number of questions asked and answered. Starting with series six, the scores were re-recorded to reflect what made the aired edits rather than the whole filmed recording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home Truths round rules
rubrics_metrics.description: "Home Truths": Panellists read out a statement about themselves, from a card which they have not seen prior to recording. The opposing team has to decide whether it is true or false by asking the panellist questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much of the comedy in this round derives from the holder of the card having to improvise answers under increasingly detailed questioning. The first series used all six panellists; from the second series onwards, the round tended to focus on the four guests. A 'possessions' element (introduced in series two) may be used where the panellist takes an item out of a box and must convince the opposing team the possession genuinely belongs to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: This Is My... round rules
rubrics_metrics.description: "This is My...": A guest comes onto the set and is introduced by first name, but remains standing in silence as the round continues. Panellists on one team tell the opposing team about their relationship to the guest; only one account out of three told is genuine, and the opposing team has to work out which it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the end of the round, the guest reveals their true identity and with which of the panellists they have a genuine relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quick-Fire Lies round rules
rubrics_metrics.description: "Quick-Fire Lies": The second questioning round, with the panellists chosen at random.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In earlier series, the panellists were ostensibly under a time limit although no on-screen indicator was ever present; the notion of a time limit was eventually dropped in later series, making the round identical to 'Home Truths' in practice. This round usually features – but is not exclusive to – Mitchell and Mack; from the fourth series onwards, the host (Brydon) also occasionally participates with both teams questioning him at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ring of Truth (former round) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ring of Truth": A celebrity fact is read out by the host, and each team has to reach a joint decision on whether it is true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was a regular round in the first three series, appeared only occasionally in the fourth series, and was then discontinued. It required teams to deliberate jointly rather than opposing-team interrogation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telly Tales (former round) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: "Telly Tales": Clips from a TV show are shown, a statement is read out about the show by a member of one team and the other team has to guess whether it is true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This round was only played in the first series and relies on knowledge or bluffing about television programmes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode running time and editing constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Each episode running time is 30 minutes, so some questions are edited out prior to airing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of editing, the number of questions that appear in an aired episode can differ from the number played during recording; production re-recorded scores from series six to reflect the aired edits. This constraint affects pacing, number of rounds, and which content (e.g., particularly funny exchanges) is kept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special episode formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Most series have included some special episodes such as Christmas specials, 'Unseen bits'/'More unseen bits', and 'Best bits'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christmas specials are themed but otherwise like ordinary episodes. 'Unseen bits' compilations gather material edited out of regular episodes and may include bloopers; 'Best bits' are highlights from the series. Series 2 and 3 combined 'Best bits' and 'Unseen bits' into a single episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format adaptability for international versions
rubrics_metrics.description: International versions typically follow the British Rob Brydon-era format closely, adapting hosts and team captains for local markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptations often retain core elements (team captains, guest panellists, rounds like 'Home Truths' and 'This is My...') while adjusting presenters and minor mechanics for local audiences; licensing of the brand/format (crediting Zeppotron/BBC) is customary.
